subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a few minutes to emphasize a couple of points in connection with this matter while we have the ears of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who we all expect will head up this new department. It has been made clear that parliament as a whole will support this resolution and will also support the bill which will follow the resolution providing there is nothing objectionable in it.
The points of emphasis I wish to make have been made time and again on the floor of this house. Some hon. members may think that we have worn them threadbare. That is only


because we have lived such a large part of our lives either in times of actual war or in times when we have been concerned over the outbreak of war. Nevertheless, we should not forget the strong feeling in the minds of the Canadian people against profiteering, either in time of war or in connection with defence preparations.
I shall take a moment to repeat this emphasis because in addition to my own conviction about it, in addition to my feeling that it is the view of the Canadian people that we do not want profiteering in defence production, there is the fact that we have in the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) a man whose yea is yea and whose nay is nay. He is a man who, when he wants to get something done, gets it done. We know that, and I think there are probably members of the Liberal party who know that if he is against something they do not get it.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Since when?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Always open to reason.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I hope the minister will not spoil the characterization I am drawing of him because I am satisfied that if there is any attempt at profiteering, if there is any attempt at patronage in connection with defence preparations, we have in the Minister of Trade and Commerce the man to stand up and say no and, if I am not mixing my metaphors too much, the man to put his foot down.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What are you looking for?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am looking for a firm stand by the minister, and I am going to quote as an authority in support of the contention that we have got to watch this sort of thing none other than the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. This is a quotation that has been given to the house a good many times. In fact the volume of Hansard from which I am reading is well worn through members turning to this page. However, I think it is well to quote it again. Mr. King was speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne at the opening of the special war session in September, 1939. I well remember being a visitor in the south gallery and hearing his speech on that occasion. At page 22 of Hansard for September 8, 1939, Mr. King said:
I come to profiteering. I believe I have already stated in this house that I know of nothing in the world more contemptible than that any man should seek to profit from the sacrifices which others are making. And if the laws and other measures which this government may introduce and seek to enforce are not sufficiently strong to destroy anything in the nature of profiteering, X hope hon. members of this house will bring to our attention, in a way that will also bring it to the attention of this country, what we ought to do to achieve that all-important end. There are some things that are very difficult

ol accomplishment. Unfortunately human nature has its weak and its bad sides as well as its strong and good sides. Sometimes it is very difficult to cope effectively with the underworld and its methods. But let me say this: I care not who the individual may be, how respectable in his own eyes or in the eyes of others he may appear, or what position he may hold; if in this crisis he seeks to profiteer he belongs to the underworld and should be treated as one of those who menace all that is sacred in human relations.
I have other quotations but I shall not take the time of the house to give them. Notably there are remarks of the late Ian Mackenzie at the time that he was piloting through the house the bill that -established the defence purchasing board in March, 1939. If I may paraphrase him, he at that time made statements similar to those of Mr. King, namely, that the government was absolutely against profiteering in time of war or in a time when the nation was preparing its defences.
As the government knows, at one time there was on the statute books what was known as the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act. It was passed in 1939, and contained a clause, well known to all members of the house, known as the 5 per cent clause limiting profits to that figure. Hon. members know that when the Department of Munitions and Supply Act was passed the provisions of that clause were superseded, and in June of last year another act was passed, namely, the Defence Supplies Act of 1950, which superseded entirely the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act.
That means that no clear-cut profit limiting legislation is now on the statute books. We have to depend for the limitation of profits and for steps to prevent profiteering in defence contracts upon the government itself, and we have to depend in particular upon the minister who will head this department. Therefore I have taken a few moments to read to him again the statement which his former leader made in the house on September 8, 1939. Not only did the former prime minister speak for all of us with regard to profiteering, but he did likewise with respect to the question of patronage. I quote again from the late prime minister's speech on September 8, 1939, at page 23 of Hansard for that special session. Mr. King said:
Then there is the matter of patronage, of favouritism. May I say this to my own following in this House of Commons:	If any of you desire to have
persons given positions, in connection with this war, simply because they are favourites of yours; if primarily for such a reason you want to have anyone given some special post, keep away from me, for I will never listen to you. I say the same to every hon. member of this house, and I say it not only on my own behalf, but on behalf of the government. We want no favouritism in this war. We want the name of this government and this country to be honourably sustained, and the man
Defence Production Act who seeks to profit indirectly by having his relatives or friends gain this contract or get that commission simply because they are among his favourites is no true friend of this administration.
As hon. members know, I am not fully satisfied that in the general conduct of affairs in this country it can be said that this government has forgotten the word "patronage"; there are too many evidences of it. However, I am not going to speak now of the practice of that art as this government carries it on in the general affairs of the country, which I deplore. But I do ask that the words of the late prime minister be taken to heart certainly so far as defence contracts and preparations for the defence of Canada are concerned. The minister who will head this department should put that paragraph on his office desk as a motto which I hope he will observe without fail.
I wish to express just one other thought and then I shall take my seat. During the discussion in September, 1939, with respect to the setting up of the department of munitions and supply, the question of the relationship between armaments and munitions on the one hand and the general economy of the country on the other was also discussed. I hope that there will be the most effective co-ordination between the work of this department, in so far as it is concerned with defence contracts, and economic policy generally. What I want to say was again said so well by the late Mr. King that perhaps the best thing for me to do is to quote him. Here again I shall read from Hansard for the special session of September, 1939. At page 172 Mr. King said:
Furthermore the experience of the last war-
Of course, he was referring to world war I; that has to be said because now the words "last war" mean world war II.
has clearly shown that the problem of securing armaments and munitions cannot be separated from the general economic organization of the country. For example, if too much energy and material is thrown into the manufacture of munitions, some other industry equally essential to the national effort may be crippled. In order to prevent such a situation arising, the governmental body must have power, not merely over the production of munitions themselves, but over production of related supplies, if a proper balance is to be maintained, and the most effective use made of our varied resources.
I know that the government is conscious of the fact that this is not a period of actual warfare. That is revealed in the nature of the other bill before us in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), Bill 24. The government is anxious to restrict, to some extent at any rate, the powers that it asks parliament to give it because this is only a period of defence preparation rather than actual war. Because of that the government

Defence Production Act is reluctant to exercise to the full such controls as were exercised over the economy during the last war. But my contention is that, in a time like this when we are upsetting the economy by the extent to which we are going in for defence production, it is important for the government to think about all those other things, the general price level, the extent to which homes are needed, and all the other things that are necessary to maintain the national effort and to maintain our national morale. I urge upon the minister who will head up this department to think in terms not only of actual war materials that need to be produced, but to think in terms of the economic picture as a whole, to attempt to guide and control it where necessary in the best interests of all our people and in the best interests of the country.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce deal with the questions I raised?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I believe it will be much simpler, Mr. Chairman, to deal with them when we have the bill before us. Then we cam discuss them in an orderly way as they refer to the various clauses in the bill.
A point that my friend was making that Vancouver is handicapped in delivering to central stores in Ottawa is, of course, true. Vancouver would be handicapped to a still greater extent if Toronto could compete for deliveries in Vancouver, eliminating the freight rates. The production of this country has developed under a system of freight rates. There are certain territories which are economic for certain areas of the country, and certain areas which are uneconomic. I think my friend will find that certain sections would be under a greater handicap in competing for war orders if the question of freight were eliminated than is the case under the present system. My officers have studied the situation, and that is the conclusion to which they have come.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Is there any way of preventing the manufacturer in the east from taking advantage of the freight rate to Vancouver, which was certainly done in this particular case? He just added on most of the freight rate from Vancouver to Ottawa, and was still able to get the contract because it was lower than the Vancouver price plus freight. There should be some way of stopping that.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I do not know what the commodity was, but it may have been a commodity in which only firms in Vancouver, Ottawa and Toronto can compete.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It was brooms.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Brooms are only made in two places. Perhaps our buyers were not very skilful in getting the price down. Ordinarily, there is enough competition in the locality to make sure that no sum that is not essential to the production is added into the cost. I would not take the broom situation as typical, as I do not think there are many products in that category.
The hon. member mentioned the subject of dispersal, and sometimes that can be accomplished. We were successful in doing quite a bit of it in the last war. For instance, explosives plants were dispersed in various parts of the country. I made very sure that they did not locate one at the head of the lakes, because I do not like the sort of plant that has no future. A good many parts of the country, however, were keen to get them, and did get them. I succeeded in locating the first big plant in Alberta to use natural gas, that is the Alberta nitrogen plant. It has had a successful post-war life, and is today an important part of the economy of Alberta.
Ordinarily putting a factory down in a small town in a distant locality involves serious problems. Suppose, for example, we built a factory employing 5,000 people in the town of Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, a beautiful town and well located for most purposes. It would mean building houses for 5,000 families, and transporting people from other parts of Canada to that locality. It can be done sometimes, but if you expect an industry of that kind to have any post-war life you have to make sure it can compete on reasonable terms with similar industries in large centres of population. Those facts have to be taken into account. It is not a matter of saying that we are going to build a war plant, so we will build it in the maritimes because they have not a similar war plant. Unless it is the type of industry that would be able to live in peacetime, that would not be a kindness to the maritimes.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Shipbuilding.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Shipbuilding was conducted in the maritimes, quite a bit of it. In peacetime it does not compete very well, unfortunately. An attempt was made to disperse industries. A good deal of study has gone into the situation. We have dispersed industries, and in some cases perhaps did not use good judgment in doing so, because some have not done so well since the war ended. We try to take into consideration every factor, and only go into the big cities such as Toronto and Montreal as a last resort.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
How serious a factor is the possibility of an atomic bomb attack? From what one reads, and from the opinions one

forms, bombing attacks would seem to be a serious factor now, more so than during the second world war. I should like to know whether the government considers such to be the case? If the minister will recall, my remarks concerning dispersal were based on the danger of attack on certain centres. Apparently the people in the United States are going to considerable expense to disperse their industries, presumably even some of the industries already established. Does the minister consider that danger is an important factor in determining what plans should be followed?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I would hesitate, Mr. Chairman, to say very much about planning an economy that would contemplate an atomic bomb attack. Atomic bombs are tremendously expensive. There are only a few of them, and not likely to be too many. It is the view of military experts that it would take a very glittering target to attract an attack by an atomic bomb. They believe that if atomic bombs were to be used in warfare there are very few targets in Canada that might possibly attract them. How to disperse industries against that sort of threat is a problem. The industry itself might form another target no matter where it was located.
I doubt if atomic bombs would be used simply to kill the civilian population. That is hardly a strategical target, but I must confess that I do not know of any effort in the United States to disperse existing industries in order to get them away from the threat of attack by atomic bombs.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The minister does not consider that is a very important factor?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I do not see how it can be cured. Atomic bombs are delivered from the air. I do not know where you could put a big plant so that it would be safe from air attack by atomic bombs.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I wished to ask the minister about the use of the iron ore for the development of Canada's steel industry. One other point had to do with the methods of checking expenditure by the new department. Can he deal with those two points?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Canada's iron ore is for anyone who wants to make steel with it. Prior to and during the last war we obtained our iron ore from Michigan. That ore has been sadly depleted. We have opened up large deposits in Canada, or are in process of opening them up. That ore will be made available to the steel makers of the world. I do not think we can close the door. These Canadian sources make it easier to develop the production of iron and steel in Canada than would be the case were the ore not available in
Defence Production Act Canada. But the development of Canada's steel industry is dependent upon a great number of factors, the principal of which probably is a market for the product. But certainly the fact that we have iron ore will assist our existing steel industry, and any future steel industry that may wish to establish itself in this country, to make a success of their enterprise.
As to the control of profits-

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I meant not only the control of profits but also the prevention of waste; that is, the checking of expenditures by the department.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We intend to follow the same procedure that we followed during the last war. We will have continuous treasury audits in the department. We propose to bring in experienced men from industry and experienced purchasing agents to direct the work; and to establish standard contract forms similar to those used in the department in the last war and which we will use in the next. All effort will be designed to eliminate waste or inefficiency. All I can say is that I think we made a fair job of eliminating waste and -inefficiency in the last war, and we shall try to do as well in the new department. The methods of the last war will be exactly the same in the present crisis, as I see it.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What about this proposed establishment of an aluminum industry in northern British Columbia?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is a private-enterprise undertaking. I understand that the project is making good progress and that certain contracts have already been placed. I judge that the work is proceeding as rapidly as can be arranged under the circumstances.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
A few
minutes ago the minister made an interesting statement which aroused my curiosity. He said that there were possibly seven locations in Canada which might be the victims of atomic attack. Does he care to dissipate that curiosity of mine by telling us where those places are?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No, I do not.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to say a
few words about this matter of decentralization. The minister has just said he thought they had eliminated waste and inefficiency in the last war. I have a shining example that I should like to bring to his attention. I agree with some of his remarks with regard to the difficulty of establishing industry at some points, but there are a great many factors to be taken into account.

Defence Production Act The minister may remember what happened in connection with processing plants for processing oil from flaxseed. Practically all of the flax grown in this country is grown in the prairie provinces. Despite the fact that we had pointed out this situation to officials under the minister during the last war, a considerable amount of government funds was provided for assistance in building and developing processing plants in this province during those years. Hon. members can see what that would mean. It meant the transportation of all of this flaxseed from the prairie provinces eastward, cluttering up an already-overburdened transportation system, and complicating the manpower problem. After the flax was processed, many of the by-products were shipped back to the same areas from which the original seed was shipped. I just mention that as one concrete example. I would not ask the minister, as he suggested, to go out to Qu'Appelle or some other beautiful little spot and spend a great deal of money in setting up some industry which would be of no use after the anticipated war period was over. But there are such features as that to which I have referred which should be taken into' consideration. It would be distinctly to the advantage of this nation as a whole if those oil processing plants that were built in Ontario here had been built somewhere in the west; for instance, at Winnipeg or Moose Jaw or some place like that, right in the heart of the area where the flaxseed is grown. It is matters of that nature that I think these officials should keep in mind.
I was amazed the other day to learn-and I am not being too critical at this stage- that of the total amount of the contracts let already in the past nine months with regard to defence purchasing, contracts for 80 per cent of it have been let within the two principal provinces of Canada. That is a high percentage, and I think it is out of all proportion. As I say, at this stage I am not being too critical. I know that things are being done in a hurry and that the whole scheme has not yet been developed. But I want to plead with the minister and his officials under him that they do not repeat the mistakes made during the past war during these next few years of preparation which we all sincerely hope is not for war but for the prevention of war. I would ask them to keep in mind the example I have just given. That was a terrific waste not only of money but of transportation, manpower and everything else. In such cases as that I hope the minister will see his way clear to expend money in the prairie provinces when a case arises such as that I [Mr. Eoss (Souris) .1

have mentioned, and in other provinces for such other matters as may seem desirable there.
With regard to atomic bombing, may I say that I think it is important that these industries be scattered so that 'one bomb will not disrupt the whole supply of a given commodity, as a result of one good shot. All these things must be kept in mind. I hope there will be a greater effort toward decentralization. The effort that is put forth from now on will be of interest to everyone in this nation, and I hope the government will try to carry it out.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I cannot allow my hon. friend's statement about the crushing of flax to go without comment. I doubt if there was five cents of government money spent in providing facilities for the crushing of flax in the province of Ontario during the last war. If there was, I wish he would tell me where. I know that a new plant for crushing flax was built at Moose Jaw, at Saskatoon and at the head of the lakes, involving large investments. I know there were plants built in Ontario, but not one cent of government money was put in any of them so far as I am aware.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think it was loans.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I will check on the matter.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: From what the minister has said, I am still not clear as to what government policy is in connection with dispersing these contracts among industries that are already in existence. He has pointed out the difficulties of setting up new industries at some points, but what about industries which are already in existence in the maritimes or in the western provinces? Is the minister's department making any particular effort to see that they are given their share of these contracts?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We try to see that the plants in every part of Canada are busy, and I think they now are busy. I know that the flour mills in Saskatchewan are busy. We buy flour from them and so does everyone else. I know that many plants in the maritimes are busy. We put radar contracts and aircraft contracts there. If my hon. friend knows a plant that is capable of making the type of things we are buying, and it is not busy, I wish he would let me know; we should be glad to look into the situation. But make sure it is not busy.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to pursue that matter. The minister has thrown out a suggestion. I have a clipping here from the

Defence Production Act
Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of this past Saturday in which the premier of the province is reported to have made this statement:
Failure of business concerns in this province to receive their share of defence contracts was resulting not only in failure of a business activity to increase, but in an actual decrease due to shortage of essential materials such as steel.
He went on to say that:
In the period ending January 11, there were 12,050 unemployed, an increase of 958 over the same period of last year.
If there are certain industries-in my own city there is a textile plant which is not government-owned. It is privately owned. They have been trying to get contracts for uniforms or army shirts, or something of that kind for six months, without success. They have been unsuccessful in getting one single item, and they have had to lay off their employees because of lack of work. Would not a plant like that be of some use to the department, particularly when it is ready to make these shirts and uniforms? They say they are competitive. Is there some reason why they cannot get some of the contracts?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
1 do not know of any reason.
Generally speaking, the primary textile industry is working at full capacity, and not able to fill the demand. I presume that this is a secondary industry, which would manufacture cloth into uniforms. There is lots of work going. A representative of that firm had better come down to Ottawa to see what the trouble is. Contracts are usually placed on the basis of tenders, but there should be work enough to go around.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
My attention was taken by the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce only a few moments ago. He said that there were only seven centres that would be worthy of the atomic bomb, and that the bombs were very expensive and hard to make. This morning I was reading an article in the New York Times of February 22, so I sent for the paper. In a lecture given in New York before the civil defence committee on Wednesday night by Dr. John R. Dunning, dean of engineering, Columbia university, under the heading, "Atom bomb output in the 10,000's seen," the following appears. If I were permitted to read two paragraphs it would give us a picture of how great the danger may be:
Dr. John R. Dunning, dean of engineering at Columbia university and one of the country's leading nuclear physicists, declared yesterday that the production of tens of thousands of atomic bombs was "perfectly feasible and possible."
His remark was made in a talk to business executives and city officials at 500 Park avenue, recruiting headquarters for the office of civil defence.
He explained later that this production would be possible if the country was willing to spend the money needed and to exert the required industrial effort.
That is as far as the atomic bomb is concerned, but generally speaking surely the minister must be aware that as a result of the experience of the continental countries in Europe during the last war it was agreed that the decentralization of industry was necessary; not only desirable, but necessary. We do not know in what form an attack is likely to come. It may not come at all by aeroplane. It may come by some other method such as the German invasion of the Netherlands or the German invasion of Norway. Ships may come into different ports with these atomic bombs in their holds and they may set them off right in the midst of the great centralized industries that we have, causing damage from which the country may take a long time to recover.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
At the present time we have
arrived, in this twilight war, at the stage where our troops are now in action, and we have embarked on a program to spend $5 billion and to double our armed forces. The people of the country are interested to know just how we stand today with this very large and important program. I do not think anybody expects the government to have a detailed plan at the present time of how that $5 billion is to be spent; but the government has been working on these ideas for some time. It is a great deal of money, and how it is to be spent is of vital importance to everybody in the country.
Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce now, or very soon, give the house an idea of just how we stand today in regard to this program? What are the government's plans in the making? We should have that information so that the people can be advised of where we are going. It is vitally important to them.
I heard today that a report came over the radio that we are to make certain types of army vehicles. It seems to me that that kind of information should first of all be given to hon. members in this house. If possible they should be advised before the press and the radio.
Will the minister give us some idea as to what the plans are, for instance, for producing planes, tanks, vehicles, guns and small arms? As I say, I do not expect detailed plans, because I do not suppose that is possible at the present time. But there must be some thinking, some preliminary plans along that line. We should like to be told whether at the present time we are planning

Defence Production Act on making these kinds of war materials. Either we are or we are not. What are the plans so far? What types of guns have we in mind, and is there any way of telling when we expect to be in production on them?
The information I am asking for is requested in all sincerity. It is not in any way an attempt to put the minister on the spot, or to embarrass him. If there are plans which the government honestly have not yet decided on, of course we cannot expect to be told, but I think the people are vitally interested in finding out what they can as to where this tremendous program is going at this date.
If we can have some sort of an interim report on these matters it would be very much appreciated by hon. members and by the people throughout the country as a whole.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Minister of National
Defence gave a comprehensive and I think a very detailed analysis of the plans of the armed services for weapons. I tried to cover in a general way the purchasing arrangements to back up those plans. Hon. members will understand that the planning, strategic planning, is not done by the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is done by the army, navy and air force, and we simply execute orders that are sent to us by those services. Perhaps the Department of Defence Production will do a little more than that. It will have funds of its own, and perhaps it will do some planning, at least of requirements. I can give my hon. friend a list of contracts and an analysis of where each contract stands, but I doubt whether that will throw very much light on the subject. I suggest that if he cares to know about aeroplanes we will be glad to tell him about aeroplanes. If he wants to know whether we are building tanks or not we can tell him that; but to give any detailed break-down of the contracts that are presently-we cannot discuss contracts in the negotiation stage without destroying the ability to negotiate.
I will try to meet his request in the discussion on the bill.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am not asking the minister for any detailed report on contracts. That naturally is unreasonable. But, for instance, on the question of tanks, I for one have no idea whether we plan to make tanks in this country, or not; whether we plan, for instance, to make any kind of vehicles in this country, or not. I heard a report that we plan to make jeeps and some sort of trailer vehicle. But that came from outside the house. I for one have heard no reports of a definite nature on vehicles. There was one report on a certain type of gun, but I have not heard anything on small arms.

If we are to make the American type of vehicles, weapons, tanks and so on it would be most interesting to hon. members and to the country as a whole to know it. speechtext:
I have a question I should like to ask, but perhaps it should be asked of an economist rather than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He has indicated it is the intention of the government to give incentive to industry to increase production through allowing accelerated depreciation. That was used during the last war, and it worked very well. But at the time we were using that form of incentive we had strict controls in this country. It seems to me accelerated depreciation is a form of inflation, and that it does increase the inflationary tendency in a country when accelerated depreciation is given on plant equipment. Immediately the money given becomes available for reinvestment.
We are not at war now, and we hope we will not be at war; but we will be going through a period of perhaps five or ten years in which we will have to increase our production. It seems to me if we are going to use

accelerated depreciation, unless we are careful in the amount of it we use we will certainly increase the inflationary tendency in the country. Am I not right when I say that accelerated depreciation has an inflationary effect on our economy?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I presume my hon. friend is quite right. As he said, it is a question which perhaps he should have asked an economist.
I would say offhand that he is correct, and that there is some inflationary effect due to the fact that capital investment is returned under accelerated depreciation more rapidly that would be the case under normal depreciation, and is therefore available for reinvestment or for spending in other ways.
However, I am hopeful that accelerated depreciation will not be a factor in the coming period to the extent that it was during the war. The reason it was a factor during the war was that we had a great deal of building to do, the building of new plants, and their equipment. In this war we start with a very strong industry. To date we have had no provision for accelerated depreciation, nor have we made arrangements for capital investments to any very large extent. We did make arrangements for capital investments in the case of a jet engine plant, and perhaps in one or two other plants. But, frankly, we hope to do our job depending very largely upon existing industry.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to commend the minister, in whom a great many people in this country have confidence. I would point out, as has been pointed out earlier today, that there is a strong feeling in the maritime provinces, one which is pretty well shared throughout Canada, that we did not receive a fair distribution of war work in the last war.
I do not know where the hon. member for York South got his figures, but the figures I have, compiled during the last war, show that the war expenditures in the maritime provinces at that time totalled $380 million, whereas those in Quebec were more than $5 billion, in Ontario more than $5 billion, and a comparatively small amount in the western provinces.
There is still some misgiving in the maritime provinces. We feel there should be a fairer distribution, and feel strongly that industry should be dispersed, for the purpose of safety. There is not full employment in Nova Scotia at the present time, a condition which I believe applies in all the maritime provinces. Many people are leaving that province looking for employment. They leave each week for central Canada, and their families follow.
Defence Production Act
That is not a proper or healthy condition. During the last war the government had the greatest opportunity in the history of Canada to make a fair distribution of industrial plants in the maritime provinces. As I have said before, they never had industries in the west, but in Nova Scotia at the time of confederation and after there were scores of industries which were purchased by central Canadian interests or were forced to close. It is clear therefore that we have suffered greatly, and no proper steps have been taken to correct matters or give us a fair share of war work.
Another matter about which I should like to speak briefly-and I have discussed it before in the house-concerns crown companies. In the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance-I cannot say which year-it was stated that $85,700,000 of capital expenditures had been made for crown industries, and that every dollar of that expenditure had been made in central Canada. Perhaps I should put it this way, that not one dollar of that enormous government expenditure was made in my part of Canada.
This is a further indication of the unfairness we have had to suffer during those years. I should like to have from the minister a statement of the contracts let up to the present time, the total amount for all Canada and the value of those let in Nova Scotia andi the other maritime provinces.
It is true that we have had considerable production of some of the heavy metals, including iron and steel. Unfortunately, however, most of that production was shipped from our province in the crudest and rawest form, to be refined in other parts of Canada, chiefly Quebec and Ontario. Rough, crude steel and iron worth $50 or $60 a ton is brought to central Canada and processed into production valued at hundreds or thousands of dollars a ton. Nearly all the war plants and barracks in Nova Scotia were demolished, while in central Canada peacetime industries were established.
Conditions such as that should not be permitted. The people in my part of Canada believe we have not had fair treatment. I have here a statement from the maritime board of trade, following its meeting last August, which states:
The executive committee of the maritime board of trade, composed of representatives of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, has passed a resolution calling on the federal government to decentralize its rearmament program and give this region of Canada a fair share of munitions contracts.
It is earnestly to be hoped that authorities will heed this resolution and that this part of the country will get a better deal than was the case

I want to jog the minister's memory on one particular item. In answering the hon. member for Cumberland he stated that a number of crown companies had operated in the maritimes during the war. Those companies were simply war set-ups. As soon as the war was over they disappeared. There was one particular plant set up during the war that was permitted to disappear entirely after the war. I think that was very shortsighted. We should have that plate mill at Sydney now. This country normally imports 90 per cent of its steel plate from the United States. The minister did a good job in putting a shipbuilding plant at Pictou. Then the minister wanted steel plates, and he
Defence Production Act took a mill that was equipped in the first war at a cost of $11 million to the taxpayers of Canada. The internal workings of that mill were brought to Ojibway falls, Ontario.
At the time of the second world war the minister will remember very well that he and 1 had a lot of discussion with respect to reequipping the mill. The minister re-equipped it at a cost of around $7,500,000. Therefore the taxpayers of Canada paid approximately $19,500,000 for the mill in the two wars. In world war II it did an excellent job, employed over 600 men and turned out steel plate for shipbuilding purposes. After that war was over I discussed the question with the minister many times in the house and said that we should keep the mill in operation. Now we are going to start to build ships again and we require plate. If the federal government did not want to use the mill after world war II I think the provincial government, if they were interested in maintaining industry in that province, should have operated it as a crown company on a provincial scale. It was a modern mill, fully staffed with competent workers, and there is an unlimited market in this country for steel plate. Nevertheless the mill disappeared again, and I am informed that the internal workings were sold this time to Czechoslovakia. Therefore the mill is in the condition it was back in 1917, a skeleton of a building with nothing inside. When there is an unlimited market in Canada for that type of production I think it was very shortsighted on our part, while we were just having a short armistice arising out of the last war, to dismantle such a plant.
If the minister decides to re-equip it this time I hope that he will do so on the same basis as he operated the arsenals. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).
He said: Mr. Speaker, if I could hope that this bill would pass second reading as quickly as the other bills that have been before us since eight o'clock, I would not rise to speak on it. I believe, however, there are others who intend to speak on the measure, so I should like-to take a few minutes to introduce it. I would not want anyone to think I am

Industrial Relations
not hopeful that at some stage of the game this bill will pass. On the 17th of June, 1948, the matter covered by this bill was discussed by the House of Commons in committee of the whole. A vote was taken on it, and I regret to say that it was defeated. There were thirty-five members of the House of Commons, however, who voted for it. The next time this measure was voted upon was on May 30, 1950, at which time I had presented a bill identical to the one now before the house. On that occasion forty-five mem-. bers voted for it. With an increase such as that every time it comes up, it will not be long until there will be a majority for it. The increase in the number of supporters for the bill, the last time it was voted on, came mainly from the ranks of the Progressive Conservative party and the Liberal party. We welcomed their support. I hope we will have still further support from these two parties when this bill comes to a vote, whether that be tonight or on another occasion when public bills are before the house.
May I take just a moment to explain the bill. When introducing it on former occasions,
I have not done that, at least not to any length, because those of us who are used to these labour matters take it for granted that its provisions are known. From some questions members have put to me, I have found that is not universally the case. This bill would add to the labour code what is known as the voluntary revocable check-off. The word "check-off" refers to trade union dues. If and when this bill becomes law, it will provide that, with respect to trade unions certified under the national labour code, it will be possible for trade union dues, under certain conditions, to be deducted from employees' wages, by their employers, and turned over on behalf of the employees to the trade unions concerned. After all, that is a common practice with respect to other matters such as unemployment insurance, income tax deductions, Red Cross and other charitable contributions. We all recall that during the war victory loan deductions were made in the same way, and I believe that Canada savings bond deductions are also made in that manner. The proposal is a simple one, merely requesting that trade union dues be deducted under certain conditions in the same way that these other deductions are made.
I would point out, as hon. members are aware, that this is something that labour has been seeking for a long time; not only labour but all the major political parties have indicated their support either directly for the check-off or in general terms for the principle of union security. While there are various
ways in which to maintain it, this is a minimum form of union security, namely provision for the check-off of union dues. I would also point out that the well known Rand formula which came out of the Ford dispute back in 1946 included the check-off. The Rand formula provided that in a plant where a union is certified to represent the employees, while all employees were not required to become members of the union, they were nevertheless required to contribute to its upkeep, which to Mr. Justice Rand seemed only fair in view of what the union was doing for all the employees. As part of that award, which is known as the Rand formula, the check-off of trade union dues was included.
Another point I wish to make is that this provision is included in the statutes of a number of provinces. I endeavoured to get together copies of the labour code of as many provinces as I could, so that in making a statement of that kind I would be able to document it. I have in my hand the labour code of three provinces in which the checkoff is definitely included. It is in the Trade Union Act of the province of Saskatchewan. It is in the act respecting the right of employees to organize, and providing for mediation, conciliation and the arbitration of industrial disputes, in the province of Nova Scotia. It is in the British Columbia act respecting the right of employees to organize, and providing for the mediation, conciliation and arbitration of industrial disputes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext: He did not hear you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
I said that the one from British Columbia was 1947 and the one from Saskatchewan was 1944. I am not suggesting that other provinces do not have that provision as well; I believe that two or three others do; but since there was not readily available any copy of the other statutes I thought I would not go any further than to indicate the ones I am sure of.
There is this wide degree of unanimity with regard to this principle of the checkoff of trade union dues. As I have said, the labour unions are for it. All political parties have said they are for it. The Rand formula contained a particularly strong argument for it; and a number of the provinces have already included it in their statutes. In

Industrial Relations
fact, I remember one occasion when this matter was up for debate previously, when a member from British Columbia, who was so accustomed to it in his province, expressed surprise that it was not already in the federal labour code. Since we are unanimous, Mr. Speaker, I suggest we should express that unanimity by writing it into our national labour code.
I may say that when the present labour code was before the industrial relations committee of this house in the session of 1948, that committee wrote the check-off into the labour code. That committee was one that gave serious and thoughtful consideration to the whole problem, and it seeme'd to those of us who were on the committee that the recommendation of the committee should be implemented by the house. When the bill came back to the house from that committee, to be considered in committee of the whole, it had in it the check-off provision in exactly the same words that are included in the bill which is now before the house. Unfortunately, a private member on the government side moved an amendment to delete that clause which the committee had written into the bill. After debate, when the vote was taken, that amendment carried and the check-off was struck out of the bill. But as I have already said, on that occasion 35 members of the House of Commons supported the check-off. That number rose to 45 last year, and it is my hope that it will not be long until there will be a majority for it.
I should point out that if this provision is written into the national labour code, as it is already written into a number of provincial labour codes, it will serve to make more harmonious and more satisfactory the relations between management and labour; and that is an objective upon which we all agree. It will serve to make labour feel that they are more definitely a part of the industrial picture in which they are engaged; and I suggest that anything that can contribute to a greater feeling of harmony and co-operation between labour and management is all to the good.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that there has been circulated to a number of members of parliament-although one was not sent directly to me-a memorandum prepared by the Railway Association of Canada protesting against this bill. I would point out that the Railway Association of Canada represents the railway companies. A number of members have shown me their copy of this memorandum; and they will bear me out when I say that practically the only argument in it is the difficult bookkeeping it would impose upon the railways which would be affected by this bill. I think the answer to this argument is

obvious. It is strange that there are no audible complaints about unemployment insurance deductions, income tax deductions, Red Cross deductions, victory loan deductions, Canada savings bond deductions and all the rest. But when it comes to making deductions for trade union dues, a great fuss is raised about the bookkeeping problem. I suggest that that argument should not carry any weight with hon. members, but rather that the railway companies would be well advised to indicate their support of this measure as a means of increasing harmony between management and labour.
One other word and I shall sit down. This measure is described as the voluntary revocable check-off. By that certain conditions are indicated. The check-off of trade union dues can take place when this bill becomes law only in the case of unions certified under the labour code as we have it. Even after that the unions concerned will have to ask for the check-off of trade union dues. Still further, each individual employee who wants to have his trade union dues deducted will have to indicate that fact in writing. It will not be automatic. It will take place only if the individual employee, on his own, requests it. Finally, it is revocable in the sense that any employee who may have indicated his desire to have his dues checked off or deducted may revoke that request and withdraw from the arrangement previously made.
As I have already indicated, I suggest that this is a minimum form of something that all parties have indicated they support; it is something that is well supported by the arguments and evidence that I have presented tonight; and I hope that when the matter is fully discussed by hon. members and comes to a vote, this time the bill will pass and this provision will become part of our national labour code.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention tonight to speak at any great length on this bill. At the outset, however, it would probably be as well if I indicated that what I have to say is in support of it.
It is true that a certain percentage of trade unions with long craft union experience have always collected their own dues, and they will probably continue to do so. The reasons for that are many. In the craft unions there is a slightly different association with the members than there is in the industrial unions. Those who wish to continue to collect their own dues are still free to do so under the provisions of this bill. The bill merely seeks to reinstate, as has already been said,

in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act a clause which was removed therefrom in the draft stages after it had reached the stage of consideration by the committee of the whole. In my opinion, the workability of the provisions of the bill would be guaranteed by the fact that the bill recognizes, in the eighth line thereof, that a trade union would be requesting that right for an employee and, as has been said by the sponsor of the bill, not only the trade union itself but its members; and would be doing so in writing. It is true that at the present time any employee who wishes to have union dues or any other form of payment deducted from his wages and paid directly to the person or persons to whom it is due can do so by signifying in writing to his employer that such is his wish. Of course he would probably have to indicate that on each and every pay which came to him, and there have been instances where that has taken place. There have been occasions when that particular matter has been decided by the courts.
This is not new legislation. The principle involved in it is thoroughly familiar to every hon. member. I should like to draw attention to the fact that it is not an unmixed blessing. It has just as many advantages for the employer as it has for the employee. I shall not enumerate them, but among them might very well be listed the saving of time, the obviating of disruption of activities within the plant, and a general simplification of the fulfilment of contract terms; consequently more harmonious employer-employee relations. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, without prolonging the discussion on this bill unduly, I just wish to say simply that it is my intention to support it. I hope that those hon. members who are now interested will carefully consider the advantages of amending the act to this extent, and thereby taking one more step toward country-wide employer-employee harmony.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this bill I think perhaps the best argument in favour of it is that it is an amendment to an act to provide for the investigation, conciliation and particularly settlement of industrial disputes. This amendment will remove one of the main causes of disputes between labour and management, without in turn causing any economic disturbance in the country or costing industry more than a few cents per month per employee. I understand that the railway unions, which come under the federal act, have offered on occasion to accept full responsibility for any charges that may be involved.
I also have received a copy of the brief of the Railway Association of Canada, but I fail to agree with any part of their submission. One of the best reasons for allowing a check-off is to be found in one section of that brief which states that their accounting is centralized while their employees are stretched out across the country, some being in small towns that are fifteen to twenty miles away from where the accounting is being done. The fact that the accounting is centralized means that only one simple punch on a tabulating card will be required to make the required deduction that could be done at very little expense to the companies involved.
It is true that this is a weak form of compulsion on the part of the companies involved. However, the present act that compels management and labour to meet and endeavour to settle their disputes is a form of compulsion. The compulsion here is no greater or no less than to require that once a union has been established the company shall give that union the minimum of union security. Union security is generally recognized and there are many decisions to this effect by famous judges and arbitrators. I have one in mind that I should like to place on the record. This is the report of the board in a dispute between Gotfredson Limited, Windsor, Ontario, and local 195, International Union, United Automobile Aircraft and Agricultural Implement Workers of America. The chairman of the board was His Honour Judge J. J. Coughlin, and I quote from the report as follows:
The board is of the opinion that the day of collective bargaining is here to stay. It is also of the opinion that of existing organizations the labour union is the best equipped to protect the interests of the industrial worker and is therefore the right kind of collective bargaining agent.

We further are of opinion that among labour unions that one will best serve the interests of its members which is governed by men of judgment and moderation and not by extremists.
We feel that no single influence is more important in bringing about the condition where men of the former rather than the latter type shall govern any union than is the friendly and co-operative attitude of management towards that union.
As I said earlier, to grant the check-off is a very limited form of union security but is recognition of the union by the management. I have here a copy of a union agreement which I had the honour to negotiate in June of 1949 prior to the general election of that year. It was the last occasion on which I had such honour. In it there is a clause governing the check-off. I should like to read it in order to show the house that there is nothing of a compulsory nature in the assignment. The assignment under section A of paragraph 64 is substantially in the following form:
The company shall honour a written assignment of wages to the union.
Section B reads:
An assignment pursuant to section A shall be substantially in the following form:
To the	company. Until this authority is
revoked by me in writing, I hereby authorize you
to deduct from my wages and pay to local	of
the	union	initiation fees	dues
	per month	
And so on. I cannot see that there is a great deal of compulsion there, certainly not on the employee. Of course union security was written into the agreement at an earlier time when I also had the honour of negotiating, and that security had been in existence for four or five years. Prior to the time the security of the check-off was granted to the union there was a measure of tumult in the ranks of labour and disagreements were more numerous. Once the check-off came into effect there was tranquillity between them and very great strides were made. There was a great deal of co-operation.. The union co-operated to the extent of allowing the company to introduce methods of job simplification. Every effort was put forward to speed up production, lower costs and so on. These things can be done, and at this time it is most necessary that there be close cooperation between management and labour.
The time has come when labour in all probability will have to relinquish some of the gains it has made over the past few years. Labour must have the confidence of management and must feel confident that management is not going to take away those rights during an all-out production effort. I am sure that if this measure is adopted there will be a great deal more co-operation, so far as labour relations are concerned, between
Industrial Relations
the railway companies and the railway employees. It might be worthy of mention at this time that the only strike that really affected the economy of Canada in recent years was in the railway industry where there is no measure of union security. It might also be worth mentioning in the interests of labour that the railway industry is far below others in the matter of wage increases since 1949. All other unions have gained their justifiable increases and the transportation industry is well down in the list. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to talk the bill out. I rise at this time for the purpose of carrying it over so that we may have an opportunity on Tuesday night to continue the discussion. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) made certain remarks tonight that require answering for purposes of clarification. May I tell him that to me this discussion seems very old. It is like going back and learning my catechism again, who made the world and that kind of thing, because it is a good many years ago that this particular measure became acceptable in my province. As the minister mentioned, many years ago the check-off was recognized in practice. It was brought to Nova Scotia from the old country. The English, Welsh, Irish and Scots immigrants, who were brought out here for coal mining in the early days when the province was being developed, brought the union idea with them and the method of collecting dues on a voluntary basis.
I know that when I started to work in the coal mines about 1908 the check-off of union dues was then a matter of course. They had even got past the period of paying dues over the counter, and the check-off was in effect when I first went into the mines, not by compulsion but by agreement. I cannot see the idea of compulsion. Every law on the statute books has an element of compulsion. We are compelled to recognize the laws of the country but the laws of the country are enacted for the purpose of protecting the great majority of the people against small minorities who want to rule as they see fit whether or not it is in the best interests of the country.
The word "compulsion" is a misnomer in relation to this bill because all laws have a certain element of compulsion. They must have. From the legal standpoint the check-off for union dues was put into the labour code of Nova Scotia in 1930 and has been in effect
642	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act there ever since. Under the terms of this particular bill there is nothing that compels a man to pay union dues. The laws of the province of Nova Scotia say that when the union and the employer come to an agreement the check-off is legal if they so desire. In the final analysis the application of the law is in the hands of those who negotiate the collective agreement, and the way that it shall be done is written into the union agreement.
If I so desire I can then go to my employer and tell him that I want my dues deducted in that way. If I do not want them deducted in that way then they are not. On the other hand, if the union misuses or abuses the privilege of collecting my dues in that way I can withdraw my card from the office and refuse to pay dues. I have seen that happen. In protest against certain activities of our hierarchy I have seen us withdraw our cards en bloc and keep them out for a long time in order to bring them to their senses. Therefore there is nothing detrimental to the best interests of the man who works.
The comparison between Great Britain and Canada is not a good one. In Great Britain there is a completely different set-up. It is the kind of set-up I would not want to have in Canada under our circumstances. While our system rests on collective bargaining, voting on strikes and that kind of thing, the British system is pithead action, strike on the job, without consultation with union officials, votes or anything else. They use it very temperately and with good judgment, but with the kind of industrial set-up we have in Canada if we had that kind of thing we would have a lot of difficulty.

Mr. Speaker, I find that my hon. friend's suggestion is a rather awkward one for me to follow, because so far as the principle of the bill is concerned or the circumstances under which the bill if passed might operate, both have been covered, first by the extensive statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the resolution stage of this bill, and secondly, by the statements by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) concerning the defence program, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) concerning defence supplies, and with particular reference to the use that would be made of emergency control legislation when passed. To those statements I do not think I can usefully add anything. If I am to say anything, therefore, in response to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) I can only do so in terms of some of the criticisms which have been made in the debate on the resolution by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming).
The suggestion was made by the leader of the opposition that the bill should clearly state the powers that it purports to give. I believe that hon. members, having now had an opportunity of reading the bill, will see that it does clearly state what those powers are. Then, as I recall his statement, he said that we should state which of those powers we were proposing to assume. It is that point which is fully covered in general terms by the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
In so far as legislation of this nature is concerned, I think that the lawyer members at least would agree that if we knew exactly what powers we are going to need to use, it would not be necessary to pass legislation of this character giving powers to the governor general in council. We would pass a statute applying certain definite powers set out in the statute and be done with the

whole matter. It is because in the situation in which we now find ourselves there is a possibility that some or others of a number of powers may be required, as developing circumstances, which are not known at the time of the passage of the legislation, may make necessary, that legislation of this character is requested, and that these powers are left to the discretion of the governor general in council. All hon. members in the chamber will recall that during world war II an elaborate system of wartime controls of one kind and another was set up, and various crown corporations as well. Very wide powers were exercised by order in council, all pursuant to an act which was passed more than twenty-five years before, the War Measures Act.
From that I think it can be seen that it would be quite unreasonable to have asked the prime minister of the day, Sir Robert Borden, when he was seeking the enactment of the War Measures Act in 1914, to state which of the powers in that statute were going to be exercised by the government.
In the present case the member for Eglinton, in a speech which, with certain rather conspicuous exceptions, I thought was an admirable one, set out four requirements for legislation of this sort. I should like to refer to what he said. He said that, in the first place, it should carefully define the emergency. In the second place, it should trespass as little as required to meet the emergency on powers that are, under our constitution, normally held by the provinces. In the third place, he says we shall wish to see that the exercise of those powers is carried out with due regard for the responsibility of the cabinet to this house. Then he says that in the fourth place, as to defence of the rights of individuals in this country, rights that have often been ignored under similar legislation in times past, there must be in this bill provisions to safeguard the rights of the individual, so that he will not be denied access to the courts.

In the first place, he said that this bill should - carefully define the emergency. If members will examine the bill they will see that it is succinctly and carefully described. The preamble says:
Whereas an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada;
It should carefully define the powers that are sought, and the duration of the powers commensurate with the duration of the emergency. If members will examine the bill they will see that the powers which are effected are practically the equivalent of the powers effected by the War Measures Act, with three conspicuous exceptions which have to do with the rights of individuals with which the member for Eglinton was concerned. The omissions are first the power to detain, deport and exclude citizens; second, censorship and control and suppression of writing; third, appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property and the use thereof.
Then, with regard to the duration of the act, if passed, hon. members will see that clause 5 provides as follows:
Nothing in this act limits or restricts the powers conferred on the governor in council by the War Measures Act and, notwithstanding anything in section four, if while sections one to four are in force a proclamation is issued under the War Measures Act declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists, sections one to four are repealed and all orders and regulations lawfully made under or pursuant to authority conferred under this act in force immediately before those sections are so repealed, continue in full force and effect as if made under the War Measures Act and shall be deemed to have been so made.
In other words, this is an act passed to cover a more limited emergency that exists at the present time until such time-God forbid that it should ever come-as it is necessary to bring into effect the War Measures Act itself; whereupon the invocation of that act will provide a continuity for any steps that have been taken under this act, and go on from that point; otherwise the act expires on May 31, 1952, under clause 4 thereof.
My hon. friend's second point is that the act should trespass as little as is required to meet the emergency on powers that are, under our constitution, normally held by the provinces. I think there will be general agreement-and I need not labour this point-that where there is a declaration of an emergency of this sort, powers that are normally within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures comes under the jurisdiction of parliament.
The third requirement suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) is

Emergency Powers Act that the exercise of those powers be carried out with due regard for the responsibility of the cabinet to this house. If hon. members will examine the bill they will see that it provides for the tabling, under the Regulations Act, of all orders in council made pursuant to this act; and that it also provides in section 2, subsection 4:
If the Senate and the House of Commons within a period of forty days, beginning with the day on which any order in council made under this act is laid before parliament in accordance with the Regulations Act and excluding any time during which parliament is dissolved or prorogued or during which both the Senate and the House of Commons are adjourned for more than four days, resolve that it be annulled, it shall cease to have effect, . . .
In other words the cabinet, in exercising its powers under this proposed act, must table the orders in council resulting from their invocation of those powers; and this bill in express terms provides for the Senate and the House of Commons the privilege of annulling the orders in council which the cabinet has passed if they wish to do so.
The last requirement of, I presume, his ideal statute of this kind which was suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton is that it safeguard the right of the individual so that he shall not be denied access to the courts in the assertion of his rights. Mr. Speaker, I think it would be fair to say that if we felt that the bill in fact accorded so completely as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) says it does with the requirements of a perfect bill suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), we would pass it with far fewer reservations than we find we are compelled to make. Unfortunately, however, we do not agree with the minister that it accords so completely with those requirements as he appears to feel that it does.
I should say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the position we take is that, having pressed for some time, and particularly since September of last year, for the government to take some action to deal with the situation which we on this side felt was in fact one of emergency, and in particular having pressed for the declaration of the existence of an emergency, we cannot under the circumstances oppose the principle of this bill which

is, after all, in the first place, that an emergency exists and that therefore it is essential that the government should have emergency powers. That being the case, I can say for the official opposition that we are not opposed to the principle of the bill and will not oppose second reading of this measure. Nevertheless, we have a number of reservations. I suppose that at this point some of those on the government side might say: That seems to be the usual story. The minister, however, has himself referred to the requirements which were suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton as being desirable in legislation of this type. We do not feel that those requirements are met as fully as they might easily be met, and certainly not as fully as I think we are entitled to expect that they be met.
In connection with emergency legislation we have always pressed for as narrow a definition as possible of the powers to be delegated. I do not mean simply to define the categories of activities which are to come under control. There is certainly some effort to do that in this bill, just as there was under the War Measures Act. The minister himself has said that, under the War Measures Act, power to do almost anything in any manner was given to the governor in council. What we want, and what we feel there should be rather than a mere classification of the categories of subjects or activities which are going to be subject to the bill, is that there should be a statement of the way in which those activities are going to be controlled, and of what measures the government intends to take or contemplates taking either in the remote or in the immediate future, to deal with the situation which they must foresee arising by virtue of the emergency which they themselves have declared and to which they now invite the House of Commons to subscribe.
But here we have no accurate definition of the emergency. When one looks at the bill, Mr. Speaker, one finds that it states that an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada. That does not seem to me to be an accurate definition of what the emergency is. In what way does it threaten the security of Canada? In what way does it make it essential to take emergency powers to deal with it? Is it because of shortages of commodities? Is it prices that the government is worried about? Is it military action which is going to have to be taken? Or what is the object of this bill, and in what way are the powers going to be used?
